questions.q: What is "physical design" in the context of this lesson?
options: Translating the logical star schema — facts, dimensions, grain — into real CREATE TABLE DDL
Choosing which server rack the database will run on
Designing the OLTP source system's original schema
Picking a color scheme for the reporting dashboard
questions.explain: Physical design is where the grain, fact type, and dimension decisions made earlier in the course become actual SQL Server tables, data types, and keys.

questions.q: Why does a fact table typically use an INT DateKey (YYYYMMDD) instead of a DATETIME column to represent date?
options: An integer surrogate date key is smaller and joins to Dim_Date faster than a DATETIME column
SQL Server does not support DATETIME columns in fact tables
DATETIME columns cannot be indexed
YYYYMMDD integers are required by the SQL standard
questions.explain: A 4-byte INT date key that joins to Dim_Date is a deliberate departure from OLTP habit, chosen for storage and join performance at fact-table scale.

questions.q: On a dimension table, why is the source system's natural/business key kept as an ordinary column instead of being dropped in favor of the surrogate key?
options: It's needed to look up the correct surrogate key during ETL loads, even though it's never the join key for reporting
SQL Server requires every table to have exactly two primary keys
Natural keys are always faster to join on than surrogate keys
Reporting tools cannot query a table that lacks its original natural key
questions.explain: The natural key is retained purely for ETL lookups (matching incoming source rows to existing dimension rows); the surrogate key is what fact tables actually join to.

questions.q: What column-type choice does this lesson recommend for a fact table's measure columns, like SalesAmount?
options: A narrow numeric type such as DECIMAL, never a text type like NVARCHAR
NVARCHAR(MAX), so any currency format can be stored
BIT, since most measures are boolean
It doesn't matter — all data types cost the same storage
questions.explain: Fact tables hold millions or billions of narrow rows; every extra byte per row (like storing a number as text) costs real space and I/O at that scale.

questions.q: According to the lesson, what indexing decision is deliberately deferred out of the fact table's initial CREATE TABLE statement?
options: Which clustered index (almost always a clustered columnstore index) to put on the fact table
Whether the fact table needs a primary key at all
The data type of the surrogate keys
Whether foreign keys should reference dimension tables
questions.explain: Indexing a fact table — specifically the clustered columnstore index decision — is significant enough to get its own lesson (Lesson 32) rather than being folded into the initial table design.
